name: Wireshark Advanced — FTP Dissection, Follow Stream, Object Export, RDP Decryption
description: Advanced Wireshark techniques: isolating FTP control and data channels to reconstruct transferred files, following TCP streams to read full conversations, exporting HTTP objects (images, files), and decrypting RDP sessions using an RSA private key imported into Wireshark's TLS settings. These workflows are core to NTA-based incident investigation.
source: CDSA Module 07: Intro to Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== FTP DISSECTION ===
FTP uses TWO channels:
  Control (port 21): Commands and responses — USER, PASS, RETR, STOR, etc.
  Data (port 20 or negotiated): Actual file content transfer

Filters:
  ftp            → control channel only (commands/responses)
  ftp-data       → data channel only (file content)
  ftp || ftp-data → both channels
  ftp.request.command == 'USER'   → all USER commands (credential hunting)
  ftp.request.command == 'PASS'   → all PASS commands (cleartext passwords)
  ftp.request.command == 'RETR'   → file downloads
  ftp.request.command == 'STOR'   → file uploads

Find cleartext credentials in FTP:
  1. Apply filter: ftp
  2. Look for USER and PASS commands in Info column
  3. Credentials are in plaintext — no decryption needed

=== FTP FILE EXTRACTION (5-STEP WORKFLOW) ===
Goal: reconstruct a file transferred over FTP from a PCAP

  Step 1: Filter to FTP data channel
    → Apply display filter: ftp-data

  Step 2: Identify the file transfer packet
    → Look for packet with large payload in Packet List
    → Check Info column for filename hint (if using RETR, it's in ftp filter)

  Step 3: Follow the TCP Stream
    → Right-click the ftp-data packet → Follow → TCP Stream
    → The stream dialog opens showing the raw file bytes

  Step 4: Change output encoding
    → In Follow Stream dialog: change 'Show data as' dropdown to 'Raw'
    → This is critical — text mode may corrupt binary files

  Step 5: Save the stream as file
    → Click 'Save As' in the stream dialog
    → Save with appropriate extension (e.g., .jpg, .exe, .pdf)
    → File is now reconstructed from captured network data

=== FOLLOW TCP STREAM ===
Used to read full conversations between two endpoints:
  → Reassembles fragmented TCP segments in order
  → Shows request and response in colored flow (red = src, blue = dst)
  → Works for any TCP-based protocol: HTTP, FTP, Telnet, SMTP, etc.

Methods:
  Option A: Right-click packet → Follow → TCP Stream
  Option B: Apply display filter: tcp.stream eq <stream_number>
    → Find stream number in blue Packet Details pane under TCP header
    → Multiple streams share the same flow — use number to isolate one

Stream dialog options:
  'Entire conversation' → both directions
  Show as: ASCII | Hex | Raw | C Arrays | YAML
  → Use 'Raw' before saving binary files
  → Use 'ASCII' for text-based protocol analysis

Hunting cleartext credentials in telnet:
  1. Follow TCP stream on port 23 traffic
  2. Read login exchange in ASCII view
  3. Look for Username: / Password: prompts

=== HTTP OBJECT EXTRACTION ===
Extract files (images, downloads) from HTTP traffic without following streams manually.

Method 1: GUI Export
  1. Apply display filter to isolate HTTP:
     http && image-jfif        → JPEG images only
     http                       → all HTTP
  2. Menu: File → Export Objects → HTTP
  3. Dialog shows all HTTP objects (files, images, scripts)
  4. Select file → Save / Save All

Method 2: Follow Stream for specific object
  1. Find the HTTP response packet containing the file
  2. Right-click → Follow → TCP Stream
  3. Show as 'Raw', save the stream
  4. Note: includes HTTP headers — may need to strip them

Filter tips:
  http.request.method == 'GET'   → only GET requests
  http.response.code == 200      → only successful responses
  image-jfif                     → JPEG images specifically
  http.content_type contains 'image'  → any image type

=== RDP DECRYPTION ===
Wireshark can decrypt RDP (port 3389) traffic if you have the server's RSA private key.
Requires: TLS private key file (PEM format) for the RDP server

Steps:
  Step 1: Filter to RDP traffic
    → Apply display filter: tcp.port == 3389
    → Confirm TLS handshake packets present

  Step 2: Open TLS preferences
    → Menu: Edit → Preferences → Protocols → TLS
    → (or right-click a TLS packet → Protocol Preferences → TLS)

  Step 3: Import RSA key
    → Click 'RSA keys list' → '+' button
    → IP address: <RDP_SERVER_IP>
    → Port: 3389
    → Protocol: tpkt           ← IMPORTANT: use 'tpkt' not 'rdp'
    → Key file: browse to .pem key file
    → Click OK

  Step 4: Refresh/re-open PCAP
    → Wireshark automatically decrypts the RDP session
    → Packets now show as RDP/T.125 instead of TLSv1.2
    → Can see mouse movements, keyboard input, screen updates in decrypted form

Note: Only works if the TLS session used RSA key exchange (not ECDHE/DHE).
Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) cipher suites cannot be decrypted with just the server key.
